title: What goes in a homeschool portfolio? Keep the evidence
dek: Choose dated work that explains what your child did and how learning developed. Build around the actual requirements, not a perfect-looking binder.
metaDescription: Build a useful homeschool portfolio with a dated activity log, selected work and clear evidence notes. Check local requirements before submitting.

sources.name: Florida Legislature: section 1002.41, home education
sources.note: Official example of required activity-log and work-sample contents. These are Florida-specific requirements, not universal portfolio rules.

paragraphs: A homeschool portfolio brings together the records and work samples needed to explain a child's learning over a period. Depending on your rules and purpose, that may include an activity log, reading-material titles, dated writing or mathematics samples, project evidence and required assessment records. Start with the actual requirements, then select evidence that is understandable rather than merely attractive.

By the time you need the folder, the kitchen experiment has been cleared away and the best explanation happened out loud. A useful portfolio is built before those details disappear. It does not have to look like a published book. It has to make the work and its context findable.

This guide is for US parents assembling evidence for their own records or a requested review. Portfolio requirements differ by educational route, location and purpose. The suggestions below are an organisation method, not a promise that every authority requires or accepts the same contents.

body.heading: Find the purpose before choosing the pages
items: Identify whether this is a personal learning record, a required evaluation portfolio, a transfer record or another specific submission.
Locate the current official instructions for that purpose. Record required contents, deadlines, retention periods and who is entitled to request or receive material.
Choose a date range and keep one child's evidence identifiable. Do not mix several children's work without clear attribution.
Select dated items that show actual work and enough context to explain what the child did independently or with support.
Check that the log and samples agree. Keep gaps and reconstructed details visible rather than manufacturing a complete-looking history.

body.heading: Choose evidence that answers a question
rows: A reading-title log, a short response or discussion note
What was read and what the child explained; not just a book-cover photo
Dated drafts or finished pieces from different points
The task, changes and any help given
Worked examples, problem-solving notes or an explanation
The idea being tested and the child's reasoning
Notes, drawings, measurements or a few relevant photographs
Question, method, observations and the child's contribution
The actual report or result required for your route
Date, provider and the requirement it fulfils

body.heading: Keep samples that explain progress, not just highlights
paragraphs: A polished final page may be useful, but it can hide the learning that got there. When appropriate, keep earlier and later examples with a brief note explaining the task. A sample corrected heavily by an adult should not be presented as wholly independent work.

You do not need to collect something impressive from every subject every week. Choose a manageable routine for saving useful evidence, alongside anything the applicable rules specifically require. The [learning-log template](/guides/homeschool-record-keeping-template) gives each sample a dated reference so you can find the supporting record.

Practical, oral and collaborative work can still be documented. A short note of what the child explained, a sketch or a photograph with context may preserve more information than a photograph of a completed object alone. Check what the particular review accepts; an attractive photo is not a substitute for required evidence.

body.heading: An invented portfolio entry with enough context
paragraphs: Suppose a child compares two seedlings over several weeks. The portfolio holds a dated drawing and measurement note, a photograph of the setup and a brief explanation of what the child noticed. The entry also says which parts were done together and which explanation the child gave without prompting.

The parent adds a later observation when the child changes the explanation. That pair tells a clearer story than a single picture labelled science project. It is still an example of documentation, not proof of a particular grade standard or a guarantee that an evaluator will accept those materials alone.

body.heading: Check local requirements without copying another family's rule
paragraphs: For a specific statutory example, [Florida's home-education law](https://wwwo.leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=1000-1099%2F1002%2FSections%2F1002.41.html%2F) describes an activity log, reading-material titles and samples of student work. That is a Florida example, not a universal definition for every state or home-learning arrangement.

Use the [requirements verification guide](/guides/homeschool-record-keeping-requirements-by-state) to separate what must be retained from what must be submitted. Check current official instructions and ask for written clarification if requests conflict. Do not send private family information simply because it happens to be stored beside the learning records.

body.heading: Ask useful questions before an evaluation

items.line: Which portfolio contents are required for this review, what period should they cover, and where can I find the current written instructions?
Some learning was practical or discussed aloud. What form of dated observation or work evidence is appropriate for this process, and what additional records are required?

body.heading: Do one final evidence pass
items: Make dates, child names and subject references consistent enough that someone can follow them without your memory filling every gap.
Check that photographs and files open, that required originals are preserved, and that the review can use the format you chose.
Separate required submissions from personal working notes. Share only what is appropriate through the agreed route.
Save the submitted version and confirmation, then use [preparing for a homeschool evaluation](/guides/preparing-for-a-homeschool-evaluation) for the appointment or process itself.

body.heading: A portfolio does not have to be a showcase

items.q: How many samples should I keep for each subject?
items.a: There is no universal number. Start with the applicable rules and the purpose of the portfolio. Then choose enough relevant, dated evidence to explain the work and any development over time. A large stack of repetitive pages is not automatically more informative than a smaller set with clear context.

items.q: Can a homeschool portfolio be digital?
items.a: It can be useful digitally, but check the format accepted for the particular review and any rules about originals. Use understandable file names, dates, backups and access permissions. Make sure a reviewer can actually open the material before assuming a shared folder or a link is sufficient.

items.q: Should I leave mistakes out of the portfolio?
items.a: Not automatically. Earlier work and a later correction can explain learning, especially when the task and support are recorded. Select evidence for the portfolio's actual purpose, not to manufacture an appearance of perfect performance. Keep any specifically required materials even when they are not the pieces you would otherwise choose.

body.heading: Make the evidence easy to return to
paragraphs: The practical goal is a record you can explain and locate. Keep the [reading log](/guides/homeschool-reading-log), daily activity references and selected work connected instead of maintaining three unrelated archives.

[Homeschooling Companion](/shop/homeschooling-companion) is an optional place to organise the learning information you enter. It is not a curriculum, evaluator or legal certification. A clearly labelled folder and the free worksheet can do the first useful job without a purchase.

research.primaryQuery: what to include in a homeschool portfolio
research.intent: Select and explain useful learning evidence without presenting one state's requirements as national rules.
sourceChecks: Current official Florida statutory text checked; legal contents are explicitly labelled jurisdiction-specific.
Saved article, audit and community research reviewed for portfolio scope and evidence-selection problems.
limitations: No universal sample count or accepted digital format is asserted.
